steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Premenstrual Syndrome focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Premenstrual Syndrome.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Premenstrual Syndrome.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Premenstrual Syndrome require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Premenstrual Syndrome.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: GFR increases by 50% in normal pregnancy; adjust renal eliminated medications accordingly.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when pruritus occurs in 2nd/3rd trimesters.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Strictly utilize FDA Category A/B or well-characterized safe pregnancy registry medications.
special_populations.elderly: For postmenopausal hormone therapy, use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; transdermal preferred.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is premenstrual syndrome (PMS)? Premenstrual syndrome, or PMS, is a group of physical and emotional symptoms that start one to two weeks before your period . Most women have at least some symptoms of PMS, and the symptoms go away after their periods start. The symptoms may range from mild to severe. What is premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD)? Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe type of PMS. With PMDD, the symptoms are severe enough to interfere with your life. PMDD much less common than PMS. What causes premenstrual syndrome (PMS)? Researchers don't know exactly what causes PMS. Changes in hormone levels during the menstrual cycle may play a role. These changing hormone levels may affect some women more than others. What are the symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS)? PMS symptoms are different for everyone. You may get physical symptoms, emotional symptoms, or both. Your symptoms may also change throughout your life. Physical symptoms may include: Breast swelling and tenderness Acne Bloating and weight gain Headache Joint pain Backache Constipation or diarrhea Food cravings Emotional symptoms may include: Irritability Mood swings Crying spells Depression Anxiety Sleeping too much or too little Trouble with concentration and memory Less interest in sex How is premenstrual syndrome (PMS) diagnosed? You may wish to see your health care provider if your symptoms bother you or affect your daily life. There is no single test for PMS. Your provider will talk with you about your symptoms, including when they happen and how much they affect your life. To be diagnosed with PMS, your symptoms must: Happen in the five days before your period for at least three menstrual cycles in a row End within four days after your period starts Keep you from enjoying or doing some of your normal activities Your provider may wish to do tests to rule out other conditions which may cause similar symptoms. What are the treatments for premenstrual syndrome (PMS)? No single PMS treatment works for everyone. If your symptoms are not severe, you may be able to manage them with: Over-the-counter pain relievers such as ibuprofen, aspirin, or naproxen, to help ease cramps, headaches, backaches, and breast tenderness Getting regular exercise Getting enough sleep Eating healthy foods Avoiding salt , caffeine , sugar, and alcohol in the two weeks before your period Some studies have shown that certain vitamins may help with some symptoms of PMS. They include calcium and vitamin B6 . Some women take certain herbal supplements for PMS symptoms. But there is not enough evidence to prove that supplements are effective for PMS. Check with your provider before taking any vitamins or supplements. If you are not able to manage your PMS symptoms, your provider may suggest prescription medicines. These medicines may also be used to treat PMDD. They include: Hormonal birth control , which may help with the physical symptoms of PMS. But sometimes they may make the emotional symptoms worse. You may need to try several different types of birth control before you find the right one. Antidepressants , such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), which may help with emotional symptoms. Diuretics ("water pills") to reduce symptoms of bloating and breast tenderness. Anti-anxiety medicine to ease symptoms of anxiety. Dept. of Health and Human Services Office on Women's Health
